subject: science
chapter_title: Exploring the Investigative World of Science

concepts.title: Science Begins with Wonder and Questions
concepts.definition: Science grows out of curiosity about ordinary things - the Grade 6 'Why' and 'How' questions mature in Grade 8 into sharper, focused questions that can actually be tested, from why dough rises to whether the world is getting warmer.
concepts.key_idea: A focused question is the starting point of every scientific investigation.
concepts.textbook_ref: hecu101.txt lines 20-60 (wonder, evolution of ideas, focused questions)
question_patterns: how does science begin according to the chapter
what makes a question suitable for investigation
give two everyday puzzles that science can investigate
why are focused questions better than simple ones in Grade 8
how did the idea of science evolve from Grade 6 to Grade 8
write a focused question about something you observe daily

solution_steps.explain: Curiosity about the world raises the first questions.
A broad wonder is narrowed until it can guide observation and experiment.
A good question suggests ways to collect evidence.

concepts.title: The Process of Investigation
concepts.definition: Investigation in science runs step by step: ask a focused question, observe carefully, design and run a simple experiment, then explain clearly what the observations show, using them to improve understanding.
concepts.key_idea: Question, observe, experiment, explain - then repeat with sharper understanding.
concepts.textbook_ref: hecu101.txt lines 40-70 (observe carefully, experiment thoughtfully, explain clearly)
question_patterns: list the steps of a scientific investigation
why do observations come before conclusions in an investigation
how does an experiment help answer a focused question
what should be done after the results of an experiment are in
explain the phrase learn how to find new facts
design a simple investigation for a question of your own

solution_steps.explain: Observe carefully and experiment thoughtfully under controlled conditions.
Interpret the results and let them improve the current understanding.

concepts.title: Everyday Puzzles as Scientific Problems
concepts.definition: Real-world puzzles hide in ordinary life - rising dough, warming climates, drying clothes - and the chapter's own worked example shows how an everyday situation can be turned into a full investigation with method and reasoning.
concepts.key_idea: Investigation practice starts with familiar situations, not faraway mysteries.
concepts.textbook_ref: hecu101.txt lines 55-70 (dough rises, world warming), 279-325 (worked everyday investigation)
question_patterns: give an example of an everyday situation that can be investigated scientifically
how would you investigate why dough rises
what everyday question does the chapter investigate in detail
why is climate change called a bigger mystery for investigation
turn a kitchen observation into an investigable question
what did the chapter's sample investigation demonstrate

solution_steps.explain: Pick an ordinary observation that raises a why or how.
Question, observation, experiment and explanation apply anywhere.
The same habits scale up to Earth-scale puzzles such as warming.

concepts.title: Roots and Kites: The Attitude of a Young Scientist
concepts.definition: The book's symbols teach the scientific temperament - the root on left pages stands for staying grounded in observation, tradition and environment, while the kite on right pages reminds learners to let ideas soar toward the unknown.
concepts.key_idea: Grounded observation plus soaring imagination together define the investigator's attitude.
question_patterns: what do the root and kite symbols on the pages stand for
why must scientific ideas stay grounded in observation
how does imagination help a young scientist
what attitude does the chapter ask learners to bring
explain the balance between heritage and exploration in science
which symbol reminds you to explore the unknown

solution_steps.explain: Root for grounded observation and heritage; kite for ideas taking flight.
Good science pairs evidence with imaginative leaps.
Learners act as investigators, not only readers of facts.
